lesson.title: One Bit to Catch a Mistake: The Parity Check
lesson.summary: A parity check adds a single extra bit to a group of data bits so their total count of 1s matches an agreed convention, catching any single bit error but silently missing errors that flip an even number of bits at once.
lesson.body:
Once bits are traveling across a link subject to attenuation, noise, and interference, some of them will occasionally arrive flipped, exactly the phenomenon that bit error rate measures. The simplest possible defense against that is the parity check: add one extra bit to a group of data bits so that the total count of 1 bits in the group, including the new parity bit, is always either even, even parity, or always odd, odd parity, whichever convention the protocol has chosen.

Building a parity bit is straightforward. Take the 7 bit ASCII encoding of the letter A, which is 1000001. Counting the 1 bits gives exactly two, an even number already. Under even parity, the parity bit is chosen so the total stays even, so a 0 is appended, giving the transmitted 8 bit sequence 01000001. If instead the letter being sent had an odd number of 1 bits, the parity bit would be set to 1 to bring the total back to even. The receiver performs the identical count on the bits it receives. If the total does not match the agreed parity convention, it knows at least one bit was altered somewhere in transit, without knowing which one.

The weakness of a single parity bit is exactly as important to understand as its strength. It reliably catches any single bit flip, because flipping one bit always changes the count of 1s from even to odd or vice versa. But if noise or interference happens to flip exactly two bits in the same group, the parity comes out looking correct again, since two flips cancel out in terms of the overall count, and the error slips through completely undetected. This means a simple parity check only reliably detects errors affecting an odd number of bits in the group, an important limitation for any link where errors might cluster together rather than occurring in perfect isolation.

Because of this blind spot, real systems often extend the basic idea rather than relying on a single parity bit for large blocks of data. Two dimensional parity arranges data into a grid and computes a parity bit for every row and every column, which can catch, and even help pinpoint, some multi bit error patterns that a single parity bit would miss entirely. Even so, parity in any form only detects that something is wrong, it does not tell the receiver what the original, correct bits were. That distinction, between merely detecting an error and actually correcting one, is exactly what separates parity, and the checksum and CRC techniques that follow it, from forward error correction, covered at the end of this sequence.

Parity's real advantage is how cheap it is to add and check, just one extra bit and a single count comparison per group, which is why it was standard on old asynchronous serial links. A classic RS-232 serial connection configured for seven data bits, even parity, and one stop bit, often written as 7E1, sends every character as seven bits of data followed immediately by one computed parity bit and a stop bit marking the end of the character, catching the occasional single bit error introduced by electrical noise on the cable without needing anything as elaborate as a checksum or CRC for such small, individual units of data.
